title: Black Sesame Seeds: 6 Health Benefits of Kala Til, According to Experts
excerpt: Nutrition scientists separate evidence from hype on the trending superfood that Indian kitchens have used for centuries.
body:
• Black sesame seeds (kala til) contain higher levels of calcium, iron, antioxidants, and lignans than their hulled white counterparts, according to nutritional analyses.
  • Dietitians recommend one to three tablespoons of sesame seeds per day — roughly 60 calories per tablespoon of whole seeds.
  • A 2025 review of 521 adults found that consuming about 10 grams of sesame daily for eight weeks led to modest improvements in blood sugar and cholesterol markers, though researchers cautioned the effects may not reflect reliable clinical benefits.
  • Claims that black sesame reverses gray hair remain unsupported by scientific evidence, despite their deep roots in traditional Chinese and Ayurvedic medicine.
  • Sesame allergies affect up to 0.9% of the global population and are a recognized food allergen in the United States.

Black sesame seeds have surged from a staple of Asian kitchens to a trending ingredient in the West, with Yelp naming "black sesame" a top food trend for 2026 based on a nearly 150% jump in user searches since 2023. Social media feeds are awash with claims that these tiny dark seeds can lower blood sugar, protect heart health, and even reverse graying hair. But how much of this holds up under scrutiny?

For Indian households, kala til is nothing new. The seeds appear in til laddoos during Makar Sankranti, in chutneys across South India, and in Ayurvedic remedies that date back centuries. What's changed is the attention from Western nutrition science — and the need to separate tradition-backed wisdom from marketing hype.

What Makes Black Sesame Nutritionally Distinct

Black sesame seeds retain their outer hull, which is where much of their nutritional advantage lies. Two tablespoons (about 14 grams) provide 18% of the daily value of calcium, 15% of iron, 83% of copper, and 16% of magnesium, according to USDA data cited by Healthline. By comparison, hulled white sesame seeds — the kind commonly found atop burger buns — contain as little as 5 mg of calcium per tablespoon versus 88 mg in unhulled seeds.

"I love sesame seeds because they pack a nice nutritional punch without a lot of volume," says Robin Foroutan, a New York-based registered dietitian nutritionist. Black sesame is "really high in specific minerals, like calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium," she told CNN, noting these nutrients support bone health, cardiovascular function, and balanced blood pressure.

Six Evidence-Based Benefits

1. Rich in antioxidants. Black sesame seeds contain higher levels of phenols — a type of antioxidant — than white sesame, along with greater concentrations of lignans such as sesamin and sesamolin. These compounds help neutralize free radicals linked to chronic disease.

2. May support heart health. A 2025 systematic review analyzing data from 521 adults found that consuming about a tablespoon of sesame products daily for eight weeks produced modest improvements in blood sugar and cholesterol levels. Sesame's unsaturated fats — both monounsaturated and polyunsaturated — may also help when replacing saturated fat sources in the diet.

3. May help manage blood pressure. A clinical study of 30 adults found that taking 2.5 grams of black sesame seed meal daily for four weeks significantly reduced systolic blood pressure in people with prehypertension, dropping readings from about 129 mmHg to 121 mmHg. A broader review found five out of seven clinical studies showed significant blood pressure improvements with sesame consumption.

4. Supports mineral intake. The seeds are an especially rich source of copper (83% DV per two-tablespoon serving), manganese (22% DV), and zinc — minerals critical for immune function, oxygen transport, and metabolism.

5. Contains beneficial lignans. Sesamin, the main lignan in sesame, has shown cholesterol-lowering, anti-inflammatory, and antihypertensive properties in cell and animal studies. Lignans are also converted by gut bacteria into compounds that weakly mimic estrogen, which observational data suggests may be associated with a modestly lower risk of postmenopausal breast cancer.

6. Supports skin and hair nutrients. Black sesame provides iron, zinc, fatty acids, and copper — nutrients involved in the maintenance of healthy skin, hair, and nails. The copper content supports proteins like collagen, elastin, and keratin. However, no cause-and-effect studies on dietary copper and beautification exist, and the popular claim that black sesame reverses gray hair has no scientific backing.

How Much Should You Eat

Dietitians generally recommend one to three tablespoons of whole sesame seeds per day. A tablespoon of whole seeds runs about 60 calories, while the same amount of tahini — ground sesame paste — is closer to 90 calories. For maximum mineral absorption, choose unhulled seeds over the polished white variety.

Sophie Hung, a California-based registered dietitian, advises that people on blood pressure medications or blood thinners should consult their doctors before significantly increasing their sesame intake, since the seeds can modestly lower blood pressure.

How To Use Kala Til in Indian Cooking

Beyond til laddoos and chutney, black sesame powder can be stirred into yogurt, sprinkled over salads and parathas, blended into warm milk for a sesame latte, or used as a coating for pan-fried paneer. Toasting the seeds before grinding enhances their nutty flavor. Zoey Xinyi Gong, a Brooklyn-based chef and dietitian specializing in traditional Chinese medicine food therapy, recommends grinding and storing sesame in a vacuum-sealed jar to prevent oxidation.

The bottom line: black sesame seeds are a genuinely nutrient-dense addition to the diet, but they work best as part of a varied intake of nuts and seeds — not as a standalone superfood. "Each different type of seed has a different profile of not just vitamins and minerals, but also antioxidants," Foroutan says.
